tier_reason: First-party wiki page (Perf) with five charts (AutoGemm SGEMM/DGEMM/CGEMM/ZGEMM and DTRSM, clBLAS 2.8.0 on S9150 driver 14.50.2 vs cuBLAS 7.5 on K40); the measurement client (src/client, measurePerformance.py) is public but no host CPU, OpenCL compiler flags or build options are stated, and the page says faster SGEMM/DGEMM needs NDA-only compiler flags and a proprietary clock tool, so it cannot reach A; no independent measurement found, so not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The Perf wiki page gives charts only and states no ratio. Values read off the chart PNGs at the largest sizes (about 5750; approximate, derived from page data): SGEMM clBLAS on S9150 in two bands of about 3600 and about 4000-4100 GFlop/s vs cuBLAS on K40 about 3050-3200 (about 1.15x-1.3x); DGEMM about 1880-1900 vs about 1250 (about 1.5x); CGEMM about 4500-4550 vs about 3050-3100 (about 1.45x); ZGEMM about 1940 vs about 1200 (about 1.6x); DTRSM about 1200 vs about 1220 (parity, the K40 is ahead at several sizes). cuBLAS leads or ties below roughly 1000 (CGEMM, ZGEMM) to 1200 (DGEMM) and up to about 2500-3000 (SGEMM, main band) matrix size.

notes: Chart readings in the record match the PNGs (Perf.img/*_s9150_k40.png); only the SGEMM crossover was understated (main S9150 band catches the K40 near 2500-3000, not 1000-2500). Shortcomings: cross-hardware comparison (AMD S9150 vs NVIDIA K40, equal DGEMM efficiency of about 75 percent of the chart's peak lines, so the DGEMM gap tracks the GPUs), not compared on the same device, 2015-era versions, NDA-only compiler flags and clock tool mentioned on the same page, repo abandoned since 2017-03-23; CLBlast (already verified in wave 8, tier B) reports beating clBLAS 2.12. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, 866 stars, 236 forks, last commit 2017-03-23, no archived banner.

tier_reason: benchmark_url was null and the only numbers source, the PLoS ONE paper (doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0208073, PMC6287823, arXiv 1412.4704), could not be opened here (journals.plos.org, www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, uwspace.uwaterloo.ca and inspirehep.net all failed DNS; arXiv blocked); WebSearch snippets confirm a Qiskit/QuTiP comparison on an i7-7700K but show no timing numbers, so no number could be checked and the record cannot stay above D. The benchmark code is public (stress_tests/ at tag v1.1), so a paper-access retier could lift it to A or B.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ 6.3 per the paper (WebSearch snippet only); Qiskit and QuTiP on Python 3.5 (snippet only). The public harness stress_tests/CMakeLists.txt at tag v1.1 defaults to CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release (CMake's -O3 -DNDEBUG) and adds -std=c++11 -fopenmp -DEIGEN_NO_DEBUG -pedantic -Wall -Wextra -Weffc++; whether the paper's runs used this default is not stated in anything seen here.
corrections.workload: Wall-clock time of a quantum Fourier transform on an n-qubit pure state (stress_tests/src/qft.cpp vs python/qft_qiskit.py and python/qft_qutip.py) and of a partial trace of one qubit from a random 2^n x 2^n matrix (src/ptrace.cpp vs python/ptrace_qutip.py; no Qiskit partial-trace script), swept by run.sh over 1-8 threads and 2-24 qubits, single-threaded Quantum++ vs Qiskit and QuTiP, plus the largest qubit count each simulates in 16 GB (harness at github.com/softwareQinc/qpp/tree/v1.1/stress_tests).
corrections.caveats: No numbers verified: the evidence is the author's own PLoS ONE paper 'Quantum++: A modern C++ quantum computing library' (doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0208073, PMC6287823, arXiv 1412.4704), which could not be opened here (journals.plos.org, ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, uwspace.uwaterloo.ca, inspirehep.net and arXiv unreachable); search snippets say single-core Quantum++ beats QuTiP on partial trace and Qiskit on QFT, QuTiP is faster on QFT, and Quantum++ fits more qubits in 16 GB, but the timings live in the paper's figures and were not seen. The harness is public (stress_tests/ at tag v1.1; removed from the current tree, whose benchmarks/ directory only benchmarks Quantum++ with Catch2). Harness asymmetries: the Qiskit QFT timer covers circuit construction, execute() (transpile and job overhead) on the first local Aer backend with shots=1, and the QuTiP QFT timer covers building full sparse 2^n propagators per gate, while the C++ timer covers only gate application; the C++ partial trace discards its result. The '8-core' i7-7700K has 4 physical cores and 8 hardware threads. Measurements date from 2018 (old Qiskit and QuTiP, Python 3.5); a 2024 independent comparison (arXiv 2401.09076, search summary only) lists Q++ at 22 qubits, below Qiskit, Qulacs and QuEST. Quantum++ is built on Eigen, the category's own incumbent, so blas-lapack is approximate; Qiskit and QuTiP are not blas-lapack baselines. The list URL github.com/vsoftco/qpp now resolves to softwareQinc/qpp.

notes: Downgrade C to D for lack of any number seen: the paper is blocked here and the search snippets carry no timings; the record's '21 vs 28 qubits' memory ceiling also came from a snippet not reproduced here. Paper-access retier candidate: public harness (stress_tests at v1.1, Release build by default) plus g++ 6.3 and i7-7700K from the paper could support A once the figures are read. Metadata checked: MIT, 675 stars, 142 forks, last commit 2026-04-17 (active), v7.0.3 tagged 2026-03-25.

tier_reason: Independent third-party multi-package benchmark (r2compchem/benchmark-qm README table) with CPU model (Threadripper 1950X, misc/README.md) and package versions stated; every Psi4 and GAMESS-US number in the record matches the table. Not A: no input files are in the repo (benchmark/ holds only three PNGs) and the Psi4 build and flags are not described; B is borderline since the suite is small (23 stars) and not well known.

corrections.caveats: Third-party community benchmark by the r2compchem group: 23 stars, 42 commits, no input files in the repo (benchmark/ holds only three PNG charts), no stated units, one molecule and one method, only Psi4 1.3 (2019; Psi4 is now at v1.11). Only the 'General test' (C20) has data; the SCF-cutoff, MP2 and CCSD(T) sections say 'The result is coming'. Defaults differ across packages (Gaussian 16 uses UltraFine grids and 10^-12 integral accuracy, Gaussian 09 FineGrid and 10^-10; GAMESS and Firefly converge on density change; RI/DF is off in ORCA, Psi4 and Turbomole), so it is not an equal-accuracy comparison, and the authors say they do not aim to rank packages. The table has at least one implausible row (Dalton 2018: 1502.0 at 1 core but 6215.0 at 2 cores), which lowers confidence in the harness. The win over GAMESS is only about 5 percent at 1 to 4 cores (derived from page data). Psi4 loses to Gaussian 09, Turbomole 7, Q-Chem 5 and ORCA 4 at every core count (for example 726.2 vs 573.0 for ORCA 4 at 1 core and 60.2 vs 45.5 at 16), and to Gaussian 16 at 1 to 4 cores. GAMESS-US is not one of the sparse-and-solvers baselines (SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse, PETSc), and the category is approximate: Psi4 is a quantum chemistry package and no wave 8 category fits exactly. Corroboration of the PySCF row: pyscf issue #1956 (user report, RKS/PBE cc-pVTZ on C6H10 with density fitting, one thread) shows Psi4 at about 45-50 s vs PySCF at about 110 s (and 190 s vs 150 s with density fitting off, where PySCF is faster); the maintainers attributed the PySCF slowness to sparse grid code and thread oversubscription (fixed for small systems in PR #1962). Forum reports (not opened) also have Psi4 slower than Gaussian and Molpro on other workloads.

notes: Numbers verified against the README table row by row (Psi4 1.3 726.2/372.2/193.2/102.1/60.2 vs GAMESS-US 2020 766.2/389.1/202.0/130.1/90.1); compile/README.md lists only 'Build-in Multithreading in Python 3.7' for Psi4 and GNU 4.8.5 plus OpenBLAS 0.3.10 for GAMESS-US. Shortcomings: small win (1.05x at 1-4 cores, 1.5x at 16), slower than most commercial codes in the same table, no inputs, Dalton row anomaly, baseline not in the category list. Metadata checked: LGPL-3.0-only (source headers say 'version 3'), 1.2k stars, 515 forks, last commit 2026-10-08.
